steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Latin has six cases: nominative, vocative, accusative, genitive, dative, and ablative. Each case signals a different grammatical function.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Nominative: subject of the verb and complement after verbs like sum (e.g. puella currit — the girl runs; puella est Regina — the girl is queen).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Vocative: used for direct address (e.g. O puella! — O girl!). It is usually identical to the nominative except in second declension masculine singular (e.g. Marce, not Marcus).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Accusative: direct object of a transitive verb, and object of many prepositions (e.g. puellam video — I see the girl; ad villam — to the villa).

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: What is the function of the nominative case? | Q: When is the vocative different from the nominative? | Q: What is the difference between the accusative and dative cases?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: It marks the subject of the verb and the complement after verbs like sum (to be). For example: puella currit (the girl runs). | Only in the second declension masculine singular, where -us becomes -e (e.g. Marce, not Marcus) and -ius becomes -i (e.g. fili, not filius). | The accusative marks the direct object (what is directly acted upon: puellam video — I see the girl). The dative marks the indirect object (to/for whom: puellae librum dedi — I gave a book to the girl

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: When translating, always identify the case of each noun — the ending tells you its grammatical role, not word order. Learn which prepositions take which case: ad + acc., ab + abl., in + acc./abl. — this is frequently tested. The dative is often missed in translation: always check for 'to' or 'for' when you see dative endings. For the ablative absolute, translate as 'with the [noun] having been [participle]' or 'when/after the [noun] was [participle]'.
